Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

vignette: Sita Patel, a 76-year-old mechanic who has spent her life beneath the chrome-glinting hood of trucks, has lived with a quiet, growing dread that first surfaced when a man began to shadow her after a routine job at the shop. The night she was leaving the workshop on a wet evening, he lingered in the alley, his face half-shrouded by a rain-slicked hat. Sita felt the unmistakable weight of his gaze, the way his shadow seemed to stretch longer than the alley's narrow beams. That night she could not sleep, and when she opened the curtains the next morning, the damp earth outside smelled faintly of wet soil-an odor that would later become a trigger for the memories she could not keep in order. The scent of earth on a freshly mowed lawn or the rustle of leaves after a storm would pull Sita back into that night's terror. In one vivid flash of a day two years later, while her husband was in the garage and she was cleaning the dusty floor, the smell of wet earth rose from the potted plants in the shop's break room. The smell pulled her mind into the alley scene, the image of the man's face, the way his footsteps had crept closer as she turned the corner. The memory was not a clear narrative; she could not explain the chain of events in full, and before she could finish the story she found her thoughts slipping away. It was as if the memory itself blocked her before it could be fully processed, yet the images were vivid, a photographic recall of that night-she could see the rain slicking the asphalt and the shadow stretching as if it had a life of its own. The intrusions triggered a state of hypervigilance that made Sita feel on guard even inside her own home. She would pause at the door, double-check the lock, and before turning away, glance over her shoulder to make sure no one was following. The feeling that the danger was still present, that someone could appear at any moment, kept her eyes glued to every corner of the shop. The memory of that one night-how she had felt trapped-fed her sense that she could be caught again. The memory was a kind of echo; each time the smell of earth entered her senses, the image resurfaced, and each time the image resurfaced, her heart hammered in anticipation of a threat that might be lurking in the doorway of the small workshop. Sita's hypervigilance, in turn, amplified her sensitivity to triggers. While repairing a truck, a sudden burst of damp earth from a leaking pipe would make her feel as if a dark presence was lurking nearby. She would instinctively check behind her, as if to ensure that the man's shadow had not returned. In the evenings, when she and her husband tried to relax in the garden, the very feeling of happiness that usually warmed her was hijacked by the memory's whisper: even the sense of contentment could be a false calm that allowed danger to creep back in. The more she stayed alert, the more the scent of soil, the rush of stress, and even a fleeting sense of happiness became triggers that would pull her into a loop of memory and threat. Sita's days had become a series of avoidance behaviors. She no longer stepped outside after rain, and she kept the shop's break room closed, even though it meant missing the small window where she could see the yard. When her husband suggested a weekend trip to the nearby river, she declined, fearing that the earthy scent of the riverbanks would awaken the image she could not fully name. In the garage, she kept her hands busy, wiping grease from the rims, because idle moments invited the memory to surface again. Each avoidance she performed strengthened her belief that staying away was the only way to keep the threat at bay. The cycle had tightened over months. The smell of soil would trigger a memory, the memory would sharpen her sense of danger, and her heightened sense of danger would make her more sensitive to the smell, a loop that left Sita feeling exhausted and frightened. She began to worry that she might never feel safe, that the terror might one day catch up to her even while she was inside her own home. The memories she could not fully recall and the images she could not articulate seemed to haunt her, a constant reminder of a night she had tried to forget. Sita finally sought help after a night in which she lay awake, heart racing, listening to the distant hum of a truck's engine, while the smell of wet earth seeped through the cracked window. She woke, covered in sweat, and decided that she could no longer live with the constant state of alertness that stole her peace. She is now hoping that, through therapy, she can understand why her mind keeps reliving that night, why the smell of soil is a trigger that has become impossible to ignore, and whether she can find a way to live in her workshop and her garden without the sense that she is always on guard.
